title: Equality, diversity, inclusion & cultural competence
blurb: The Equality Act 2010 and its nine protected characteristics, direct and indirect discrimination, reasonable adjustments, interpreters, cultural competence and microaggressions.
question: A practice only takes bookings by phone. A deaf patient complains that she cannot make an appointment, and a colleague says 'the rule is the same for everyone, so it's fair'. Is your colleague right, and what does the law expect the practice to do?

teach.body: Equality means everyone has a fair chance of good care. Diversity means recognising and valuing the differences between people. Inclusion means everyone feels welcome and able to take part. Equity means giving people different support so they can reach the same outcome. In Great Britain these ideas are backed by the Equality Act 2010, which protects patients and staff from discrimination. GDC standards and the dental nurse's duties both require you to practise in a non-discriminatory, inclusive way.

letters.sub: Including colour, nationality, ethnic or national origin
Protected at work, not when receiving services
Including having no religion or belief

teach.caption: Think 'Gramps' doctors'. Things like social class, accent or income are not protected characteristics in their own right, but treating people unfairly for them is still unprofessional.

teach.text: 'Same rule for everyone' is not automatically fair. A policy that applies to all but puts one group at a disadvantage is indirect discrimination unless it can be justified.

teach.body: The Equality Act requires services to make reasonable adjustments so disabled people are not at a substantial disadvantage. This covers physical features (a ramp, a ground-floor surgery), ways of working (longer appointments, quiet times, text or email booking) and extra aids (a hearing loop, large print, easy-read leaflets). The duty is anticipatory: plan ahead rather than wait for a complaint. The best way to find barriers is to ask patients about their experience and act on what they say.

teach.caption: Inclusive practice uses equity to achieve equality of access and outcome.

teach.body: Cultural competence is understanding how culture, beliefs and language shape health choices, and adapting care respectfully. Patients may prefer a clinician of the same sex, a chaperone, or appointments that fit around fasting or prayer. Use the patient's chosen name and pronouns and update the record when asked, for example for a transgender patient. For language barriers, use a professional interpreter. Avoid relying on family, especially children. A colleague should only interpret if competent with clinical information. Postpone non-urgent treatment until interpreting support is available.

rows.label: Giving up on a name: 'I'll just call you Sam'
Assuming an older patient won't want implants
'How would you like me to say your name?'
Using the name and pronouns the patient gives

teach.note: Microaggressions are everyday comments or actions, often unintended, that signal someone is different or less welcome. GDC guidance expects you to challenge discrimination and microaggressions, and to recognise your own unconscious bias.

steps.sub: Check the person affected is OK

steps.label: Challenge or escalate
steps.sub: Calmly, or tell a senior colleague

steps.label: Record
steps.sub: Write down what you saw and heard

steps.label: Report
steps.sub: Follow the practice policy; raise a concern if unresolved

items: Equality Act 2010: nine protected characteristics, GRAMPS DRS.
Direct = treated worse because of a characteristic. Indirect = a neutral rule that disadvantages a group.
Reasonable adjustments are a legal duty and should be planned in advance.
Use professional interpreters; postpone non-urgent care if none is available.
Use chosen names and pronouns, challenge microaggressions and check your own bias.

summary: You can now name the nine protected characteristics, tell direct from indirect discrimination, explain reasonable adjustments and equity, use interpreters appropriately, respect names, pronouns and cultural needs, and respond to microaggressions and discrimination in the practice.

A.q: During a team meeting on the equality policy, which of these is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010?
options: Social class
Religion or belief
Political party membership
Postcode area
A.why: Religion or belief, including having no belief, is one of the nine protected characteristics.

whyNot.0: Social class is not one of the nine protected characteristics.
whyNot.2: Membership of a political party is not listed as a protected characteristic.
whyNot.3: Where someone lives is not a protected characteristic.

A.q: A practice only accepts bookings by phone, which deaf patients cannot use. What type of discrimination could this be?
options: Direct discrimination
Victimisation
Indirect discrimination
Harassment
A.why: A rule applied to everyone that puts a group at a particular disadvantage is indirect discrimination, unless it can be justified.

whyNot.0: Direct discrimination is treating someone worse because of a characteristic; this rule is neutral on its face.
whyNot.1: Victimisation is treating someone badly because they complained about discrimination.
whyNot.3: Harassment is unwanted conduct that violates dignity, such as offensive remarks.

A.q: A patient's first language isn't English and no interpreter can be arranged today. The treatment is not urgent. What should you do?
options: Ask her young son to translate
Proceed using gestures and pictures
Treat her and explain at the next visit
Postpone until an interpreter is booked
A.why: Valid consent needs understanding, so non-urgent treatment should wait until proper interpreting support is in place.

whyNot.0: Children should not interpret clinical information; it is unreliable and inappropriate.
whyNot.1: Gestures alone cannot ensure she understands the risks and options.
whyNot.2: Treating without understanding means consent is not valid.

B.q: A transgender patient's record shows a name he no longer uses. What is most appropriate?
options: Ask how he wishes to be addressed; update it
Keep the old name, as it is on his NHS record
Use no name at all to avoid offence
Ask him to bring legal proof of the change
B.why: Using the patient's chosen name and updating the record shows respect and supports dignity, a core GDC expectation.

whyNot.1: Continuing to use a name he no longer uses is disrespectful and can cause distress.
whyNot.2: Avoiding his name is impersonal and doesn't solve the record problem.
whyNot.3: There is no requirement for legal proof before using a patient's chosen name.

B.q: A colleague asks a patient, 'But where are you really from?' How is this best described?
options: Friendly small talk
Cultural competence
A reasonable adjustment
A microaggression
B.why: It implies the patient doesn't belong, which is a typical microaggression, even if the colleague meant no harm.

whyNot.0: However well meant, it singles the patient out as different.
whyNot.1: Cultural competence means adapting care respectfully, not questioning someone's origins.
whyNot.2: Reasonable adjustments remove barriers for disabled people; this is unrelated.

B.q: A patient needs a longer appointment because of a disability. How should the practice view this?
options: As special treatment other patients may resent
As a reasonable adjustment for equal access
As something to offer only on quiet days
As a reason to charge a higher private fee
B.why: A longer appointment removes a barrier caused by disability, which is exactly what reasonable adjustments are for.

whyNot.0: Adjustments are about fairness and equal access, not favouritism.
whyNot.2: The duty to adjust doesn't depend on how busy the practice is.
whyNot.3: Charging disabled patients extra for an adjustment would be discriminatory.

C.q: You speak the same language as a patient and are asked to interpret. What should be considered first?
options: Whether the patient has already paid for the visit
Whether your nurse training makes you qualified
Whether you can convey clinical details accurately
Whether the dentist will speak slowly enough
C.why: Interpreting clinical information needs accuracy. Only interpret if you are competent to convey risks, options and consent clearly.

whyNot.0: Payment has nothing to do with whether interpreting is safe.
whyNot.1: Dental nurse training does not by itself make you a competent interpreter.
whyNot.3: Speaking slowly helps, but the key issue is whether the meaning is conveyed accurately.

C.q: Which is the best example of direct discrimination?
options: Refusing to register a patient for her religion
Taking bookings by phone only, for every patient
Having stairs as the only route to the surgery
Offering appointment information in English only
C.why: Treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic, here religion, is direct discrimination.

whyNot.1: A phone-only rule applies to all, so it is potential indirect discrimination.
whyNot.2: Stairs are a physical barrier needing reasonable adjustment, not direct discrimination.
whyNot.3: A language barrier is addressed with interpreters and translated information; it is not direct discrimination on its own.

C.q: A practice wants to find out what barriers its patients face. Which action works best?
options: Assume the barriers based on the local population
Wait until a patient makes a formal complaint
Ask patients about their experience and act on it
Copy the access policy of a nearby practice
C.why: Asking patients directly, then acting on their feedback, identifies real barriers and shows the duty to adjust is taken seriously.

whyNot.0: Assumptions can miss real barriers and reinforce stereotypes.
whyNot.1: The duty to make adjustments is anticipatory, so waiting for complaints is too late.
whyNot.3: Another practice's patients and building may have very different needs.

reteach.title: Fair isn't always the same
reteach.question: Three people of different heights try to watch a match over a fence. Giving each one the same box helps the middle one but not the shortest. What would actually be fair?

blocks.body: Giving everyone one box is equality of input, but the shortest person still can't see. Giving each person the number of boxes they need is equity, and now everyone can watch. In the practice, the 'boxes' are reasonable adjustments: a longer appointment, an interpreter, text booking, a ground-floor room. A rule that gives everyone the same box, like phone-only booking, can leave people out. That is indirect discrimination.

blocks.text: Direct discrimination generally can't be justified (age is the main exception). Indirect discrimination can only be justified if the rule is a proportionate way of achieving a legitimate aim, which a phone-only booking rule is very unlikely to be.

explain.body: Gender reassignment, Race, Age, Marriage and civil partnership, Pregnancy and maternity, Sex, Disability, Religion or belief, Sexual orientation: GRAMPS DRS.

test.q: Which of the following is NOT a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010?
options: Pregnancy and maternity
Gender reassignment
Educational background
Sexual orientation
test.why: Educational background is not one of the nine protected characteristics.

explain.body: Direct: treating someone worse because of a protected characteristic. Indirect: a rule that applies to everyone but disadvantages a group. Harassment and victimisation are also unlawful, as is failing to make reasonable adjustments.

test.q: A practice bans all head coverings in the waiting room, which affects patients who wear them for religious reasons. What is this likely to be?
options: Victimisation
Indirect discrimination
A reasonable adjustment
Direct discrimination
test.why: The rule applies to everyone but particularly disadvantages people of certain religions, which makes it indirect discrimination unless justified.

whyNot.0: Victimisation involves punishing someone for raising discrimination.
whyNot.2: Reasonable adjustments remove barriers; this rule creates one.
whyNot.3: The rule doesn't target a religion directly; it is a neutral rule with an unequal effect.

explain.body: Use professional interpreters. Avoid relying on family members, especially children. A colleague should only interpret if competent with clinical information. If no interpreter is available and treatment isn't urgent, postpone it.

children.label: Proceed
children.sub: Speak to the patient, not the interpreter

test.q: Who is the most appropriate person to interpret during a consent discussion?
options: The patient's 12-year-old daughter
A professional interpreter
Any receptionist who speaks the language
A friend in the waiting room
test.why: A professional interpreter can convey clinical details accurately and impartially, which is vital for valid consent.

whyNot.0: Children should not interpret clinical information.
whyNot.2: Speaking a language doesn't mean someone can interpret clinical information accurately.
whyNot.3: A friend may not be accurate or impartial, and confidentiality is a concern.

explain.body: Adapt care to respect culture and beliefs, use chosen names and pronouns, and recognise your own unconscious bias. Microaggressions are everyday remarks that signal someone doesn't belong. Challenge them calmly or report them.

test.q: A patient has a name you find hard to pronounce. What is the most inclusive response?
options: Ask how they would like it said
Use their first initial instead
Give them a simpler nickname
Avoid using their name at all
test.why: Asking how to say their name shows respect and avoids the microaggression of changing or avoiding it.

whyNot.1: Replacing their name with an initial avoids the effort of learning it.
whyNot.2: Giving someone a nickname without asking is a common microaggression.
whyNot.3: Avoiding their name is impersonal and can make them feel excluded.
